title: Judges 11:34–40
context: Jephthah returns home, and his only child, his daughter, comes out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. He tears his clothes, saying he cannot go back on his vow. She tells him to do what he promised, and asks for two months to go to the mountains with her companions and bewail her virginity. When she returns, he does to her according to his vow. The text adds that she was a virgin, and it records a yearly custom in which the daughters of Israel commemorated her for four days. Interpreters in both traditions are divided. Many read the passage as a literal burnt offering, a tragic act that the law forbade (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). Others read it as her dedication to lifelong unmarried service to the LORD, pointing to the stress on her virginity in verses 37–39. Neither reading belongs to one tradition, and the notes declare no winner. Both traditions agree the vow was rash and that God did not require it. They agree the daughter’s dignity and faithfulness deserve honor, and that Hebrews 11:32 commends Jephthah’s faith without approving every act.

verses.text: Jephthah came to Mizpah to his house; and behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child. Besides her he had neither son nor daughter.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah returns to Mizpah, and his daughter, his only child, comes out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. The moment of joy becomes the moment of grief.

Arminian readers note the poignancy of the scene: the daughter celebrates her father’s victory, unaware of what his vow means for her.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the text emphasizes she was his only child, deepening the tragedy and recalling the language of other only children in Scripture.

Both traditions read the scene with compassion and honor the daughter’s joy and innocence.

verses.text: When he saw her, he tore his clothes, and said, “Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you are one of those who trouble me; for I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I can’t go back.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah tears his clothes and says she has brought him very low, because he has opened his mouth to the LORD and cannot go back. His grief is real, but his words place blame on her.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah’s rash vow, not his daughter, is the cause of the tragedy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the law allowed people vowed to the LORD to be redeemed with a payment (Leviticus 27:1–8), a provision Jephthah does not seem to consider.

Both traditions read his grief soberly, as the fruit of his own rash words.

verses.text: She said to him, “My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to that which has proceeded out of your mouth, because the LORD has taken vengeance for you on your enemies, even on the children of Ammon.”
verses.arminianNotes:
His daughter tells him to do according to what he vowed, because the LORD has given him vengeance on Ammon. She accepts his word.

Arminian readers note the daughter’s remarkable faithfulness and courage, honoring both her father and the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that her response focuses on God’s deliverance, showing a faith that puts God’s work above her own life.

Both traditions honor her dignity and faith, while recognizing that her submission does not make the vow right.

verses.text: Then she said to her father, “Let this thing be done for me. Leave me alone two months, that I may depart and go down on the mountains, and bewail my virginity, I and my companions.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She asks for two months to go to the mountains with her companions and bewail her virginity. Her request focuses on her unmarried state.

Arminian readers are themselves divided here: some see the focus on virginity as pointing to lifelong dedicated service, while others take it as mourning that she will die without marriage or children.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers are likewise divided along the same two lines, and neither reading is a mark of the tradition. The stress on her virginity is a real textual hook that every interpreter must weigh.

Both traditions honor her request for time to grieve with her friends.

verses.text: He said, “Go.” He sent her away for two months; and she departed, she and her companions, and mourned her virginity on the mountains.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah lets her go for two months, and she mourns her virginity with her companions on the mountains. Her grief is shared.

Arminian readers note the companionship of the other young women, a sign of community in sorrow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the text gives space to her lament, treating her loss as real and worthy of mourning.

Both traditions affirm the value of grieving together and see in the daughter’s companions a model of compassion.

verses.text: At the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow which he had vowed. She was a virgin. It became a custom in Israel
verses.arminianNotes:
After two months she returns, and he does according to his vow; she was a virgin, and a custom arises in Israel. The Hebrew says literally that she had not known a man.

Arminian readers note that those who favor the dedication reading point to this clause, while those who favor the sacrifice reading see it as underscoring the tragedy of a life cut short.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the law forbade child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31), which interpreters in both camps weigh: some see it as making a literal sacrifice unthinkable, others as showing how far Israel had fallen in this period.

Both traditions present the outcome as disputed, declare no winner, and agree the vow was rash.

verses.text: that the daughters of Israel went yearly to celebrate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year.
verses.arminianNotes:
The daughters of Israel went yearly to commemorate Jephthah’s daughter for four days. Her memory was honored.

Arminian readers note that the yearly remembrance gives her a lasting place in Israel’s memory, honoring her faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the custom shows Israel’s recognition of her dignity and the tragedy of what happened. The exact meaning of the Hebrew verb the WEB renders celebrate is debated.

Both traditions honor the daughter and see in the remembrance a refusal to let her be forgotten.
